Fix an object $C$ of a category $\mathcal C$. Two monomorphisms $m:A\to C$ and $n:B\to C$ ([[def-monomorphism-and-epimorphism]]) **mutually factor** when there are morphisms $u:A\to B$ and $v:B\to A$ such that
$$m=n\circ u,\qquad n=m\circ v.$$
A **subobject of $C$** is an equivalence class of monomorphisms into $C$ under mutual factorisation. The class represented by $m$ is denoted $[m]$. For representatives, write $[m]\le[n]$ when $m$ factors through $n$.

Dually, two epimorphisms $q:C\to Q$ and $r:C\to R$ mutually factor when $r=u\circ q$ and $q=v\circ r$ for suitable $u:Q\to R$ and $v:R\to Q$. A **quotient object of $C$** is an equivalence class of epimorphisms out of $C$. Quotients are ordered by $[q]\le[r]$ when $r$ factors through $q$, the orientation dual to that for subobjects.

The equivalence-relation and representative-independence obligations are discharged by [[thm-mutual-factorisation-defines-subobject-and-quotient-object-equivalence]].

**What $[m]$ is, and what it is not.** The monomorphisms into $C$ generally form a proper class — already in $\mathbf{Set}$, where every singleton admits a monomorphism into a one-point set — so $[m]$ is a class and not a set. Under this development's convention a class abbreviates a formula and is not an additional entity ([[def-language-of-set-theory]]), so $[m]$ is never a member of anything and the subobjects of $C$ are never gathered into a collection. Every statement written with the bracket notation below is shorthand for a statement about representatives: $[m]\le[n]$ means that $m$ factors through $n$, which the next two items show depends only on the two classes, and $[m]=[n]$ means that $m$ and $n$ mutually factor. Size conditions on subobjects are likewise stated on representatives later on this page, never by measuring a collection of classes.

Let $[m]$ be a subobject of an object $A$ in an abelian category, represented by
a monomorphism $m:M\to A$. The **quotient of $A$ by $[m]$** is the quotient
object represented by the cokernel of $m$:

$$A/[m]:=\operatorname{coker}(m).$$

Because every monomorphism is the kernel of its cokernel
([[thm-every-monomorphism-is-the-kernel-of-its-cokernel]]), this quotient is
the object paired with the given subobject by the kernel-cokernel
correspondence. The next item checks that the definition does not depend on the
chosen representative of the class $[m]$.

Let $f:A\to A'$ be a morphism in an abelian category.

If $b:B\rightarrowtail A$ represents a subobject of $A$, its **direct image**
along $f$ is the subobject of $A'$ represented by the image inclusion of the
composite

$$B\rightarrowtail A\xrightarrow{f}A'.$$

It is denoted $f_*B$.

If $c:C\rightarrowtail A'$ represents a subobject of $A'$, its **inverse image**
along $f$ is the subobject of $A$ represented by the pullback of $c$ along $f$
([[def-pullbacks-and-pushouts]]). It is denoted $f^*C$.

The representative-independence of these assignments is discharged by
[[thm-direct-and-inverse-image-of-subobjects-form-a-galois-connection]].

Let $f:A\to A'$ be a morphism in an abelian category. Then the direct-image map

$$f_*:\operatorname{Sub}(A)\to\operatorname{Sub}(A')$$

and the inverse-image map

$$f^*:\operatorname{Sub}(A')\to\operatorname{Sub}(A)$$

form a Galois connection:

$$f_*B\le C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B\le f^*C.$$

In a pullback square in an abelian category

```tikzcd
P \arrow[r, "\beta"] \arrow[d, "\alpha"'] & B \arrow[d, "e"] \\
A \arrow[r, "f"'] & C,
```

if $e$ is epic, then $\alpha$ is epic.

For every morphism $f:A\to B$ in an abelian category, there is a canonical
isomorphism

$$A/\ker(f)\;\cong\;\operatorname{im}(f).$$

Let $C\le B\le A$ be subobjects in an abelian category. Then there is a
canonical isomorphism

$$(A/C)/(B/C)\;\cong\;A/B.$$

In an abelian category, every monomorphism is the kernel of its cokernel, and
dually every epimorphism is the cokernel of its kernel.

citations.quote: Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.

Let $T$ have split characteristic polynomial. For each eigenvalue $\lambda$, put
$$\rho_k(\lambda)=\operatorname{rank}(T-\lambda I)^k\qquad(k\ge0).$$
Then for every $k\ge1$, the number of Jordan blocks for $\lambda$ of size exactly $k$ is
$$\rho_{k-1}(\lambda)-2\rho_k(\lambda)+\rho_{k+1}(\lambda).$$
Consequently the ranks of all shifted powers determine the Jordan form uniquely up to permutation of its blocks. On the zero space the rank data and block multiset are empty.

For $m\ge1$ and $\lambda\in F$, the **Jordan block** $J_m(\lambda)$ is the $m\times m$ matrix with $\lambda$ on the diagonal, $1$ on the superdiagonal, and $0$ elsewhere.

Let $T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. A **Jordan string of length $m$ for $T$ at $\lambda$** is an ordered list $(v_1,\ldots,v_m)$ satisfying
$$(T-\lambda I)v_1=0,\qquad (T-\lambda I)v_j=v_{j-1}\quad(2\le j\le m).$$
Its **initial vector** is $v_1$ and its **terminal vector** is $v_m$. The initial vector is required to be nonzero; consequently every vector in the string is nonzero. In the ordered basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_m)$, the restriction of $T$ to the string's span has matrix $J_m(\lambda)$ under the coordinate-column convention ([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]).

A Jordan string for a nilpotent endomorphism means a string at $\lambda=0$.

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix
$$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$
the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$

Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus

Every object of $\mathcal J_k$ is isomorphic to a unique direct sum
$I_\lambda=I_{\lambda_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus I_{\lambda_s}$, where
$\lambda$ is a partition. The unique simple object is $S=I_1$.

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix
$$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$
the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

finite field, with
$$ g^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(q)=G^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(q). $$
A coefficient is zero unless $|\lambda|=|\mu|+|\nu|$.

Define the **generic Jordan-quiver Hall algebra** by
$$ H_{\mathrm{gen}}:=\bigoplus_\lambda\mathbb Z[t]u_\lambda, \qquad u_\mu*u_\nu:=\sum_\lambda G^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(t)u_\lambda, $$
giving $u_\lambda$ degree $|\lambda|$ and $t$ degree $0$.
The size condition above makes this a graded algebra.
Then $H_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is a commutative associative unital algebra and a free
polynomial algebra over $\mathbb Z[t]$ on the classes
$u_{(1^r)}$, $r\ge1$. After extending scalars to
$\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$, the assignment
$$ \Phi_t(u_{(1^r)})=t^{-r(r-1)/2}e_r $$
for every $r\ge1$, and $\Phi_t(u_\varnothing)=1$, extends uniquely to a
graded algebra isomorphism
$$ H_{\mathrm{gen}}\otimes_{\mathbb Z[t]}\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}] \;\cong\; \Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}], $$
where $\Lambda$ is the stable graded ring of symmetric functions.

For the nilpotent Jordan representation $I_\lambda$ over $\mathbb F_q$,
write $m_r=\#\{i:\lambda_i=r\}$ and $n(\lambda)=\sum_i(i-1)\lambda_i$.
Then
$$ a_\lambda(q):=|\operatorname{Aut}(I_\lambda)|=q^{|\lambda|+2n(\lambda)}\prod_{r\ge1}\prod_{j=1}^{m_r}(1-q^{-j}). $$
In particular $a_\varnothing(q)=1$.

For $r\ge1$, let $p_r\in\Lambda^r$ be the compatible sequence of finite
power-sum polynomials $p_r(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=\sum_{i=1}^N x_i^r$
([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]). For a
partition $\lambda$, set $p_\lambda:=\prod_i p_{\lambda_i}$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Write
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$ and
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda^d$. Then
$$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\ldots],$$
and for every $d\ge0$, the family $\{p_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$ is a
$\mathbb Q$-basis of $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$. These families are not in
general $\mathbb Z$-bases of $\Lambda^d$: in degree two,
$h_2=\tfrac12(p_{(1,1)}+p_{(2)})$ has nonintegral coordinates in the power-sum
basis.

For $d\ge0$ and each partition $\lambda\vdash d$, let $m_\lambda\in\Lambda^d$
be the compatible sequence whose rank-$N$ projection is the monomial orbit
sum $m_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ when $\ell(\lambda)\le N$, and is zero
otherwise. Then $\{m_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$ is a $\mathbb Z$-basis of
$\Lambda^d$.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

For all partitions $\lambda$ and $\mu$ of the same integer $n$,
$$\lambda\unrhd\mu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\mu'\unrhd\lambda'.$$

Let $s$ be an indeterminate and work in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q(s)}$,
the scalar extension of [[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]].
For a partition $\lambda$, let $m_r(\lambda)$ be the multiplicity of its
part $r$, and put
$$ z_\lambda=\prod_{r\ge1}r^{m_r(\lambda)}m_r(\lambda)!,\qquad b_\lambda(s)=\prod_{r\ge1}\prod_{j=1}^{m_r(\lambda)}(1-s^j),\qquad n(\lambda)=\sum_{i\ge1}(i-1)\lambda_i. $$
The **Hall–Littlewood scalar product** is the symmetric bilinear form with
$$ \langle p_\lambda,p_\mu\rangle_s=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_\lambda\prod_i(1-s^{\lambda_i})^{-1}. $$
This defines a nondegenerate form, because the power sums are a rational
basis ([[prop-power-sums-form-a-rational-not-integral-stable-basis]]) and
all displayed diagonal entries are nonzero. Different degrees are orthogonal;
empty products are $1$, so $\langle1,1\rangle_s=1$.

The **monic Hall–Littlewood functions** $P_\lambda(x;s)$ are characterized by
$$ P_\lambda=m_\lambda+\sum_{\mu\lhd\lambda}c_{\lambda\mu}(s)m_\mu,\qquad \langle P_\lambda,P_\mu\rangle_s=0\quad(\lambda\ne\mu), $$
where $\lhd$ is strict dominance ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]])
and the monomials use [[thm-monomial-symmetric-functions-form-the-integral-stable-basis]].
Existence, uniqueness, and the norm formula
$\langle P_\lambda,P_\lambda\rangle_s=b_\lambda(s)^{-1}$ are proved in
[[thm-jordan-hall-pairing-and-hall-littlewood-basis]], rather than assumed
in this definition. Set $Q_\lambda=b_\lambda(s)P_\lambda$.
For a real parameter $0<s<1$ the same formulas specialize wherever used
below; the theorem proves their regularity there. This form differs from
the ordinary symmetric-function Hall inner product, whose power-sum norms
are $z_\lambda$.

Write $P := \{\, x \in \mathbb{Z} : x \text{ is prime} \,\}$ ([[def-prime]]), and
take finite products in the commutative monoid $(\mathbb{Z},\cdot,1)$ of
[[lem-units-of-z]] as in [[def-monoid-finite-product]].

1. For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every list $p : n \to \mathbb{Z}$ of primes
   there is a prime $q$ with $q \ne p_i$ for every $i < n$.
2. Consequently $P$ is **not finite**: there is no $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with
   $P \approx m$ ([[def-countable]], [[def-equinumerous]]).

Clause 1 holds at $n = 0$ as well, where the empty product is $1$ and the witness
produced by the proof is a prime divisor of $2$.

For every prime $p$, the operations of addition and multiplication on
$\mathbb Z/p$ make it a field ([[def-field]]).

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Every class in $\mathbb Z/n$
([[def-integers-modulo-n]]) contains exactly one integer $r$ with
$0\le r<n$. Consequently the map

$$r\longmapsto[r]_n\qquad(0\le r<n)$$

is a bijection from the von Neumann natural $n$ to $\mathbb Z/n$, and
$|\mathbb Z/n|=n$. This includes $n=1$, where the only representative is $0$.
For $n=0$, the map $a\mapsto[a]_0$ is a bijection $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/0$.

A nonzero real polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct real roots. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-real-polynomial-factor-at-a-root]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

A **commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra** here means a commutative ring $R$ equipped with a unital ring homomorphism $\mathbb Q\to R$. We identify each rational with its image in $R$.

For $u\in xR\llbracket x\rrbracket$, define

$$\exp(u):=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{u^n}{n!},\qquad \log(1+u):=\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n-1}\frac{u^n}{n}.$$

For $c\in R$, define the **formal binomial power**

$$(1+u)^c:=\exp\bigl(c\log(1+u)\bigr).$$

Since $\operatorname{ord}_x(u^n)\ge n$, each displayed family is summable. The unit criterion makes $1+u$ a unit. These symbols name formal series only; no analytic exponential, logarithm, branch, or convergence is involved.

In a commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra $R$, for $u,v\in xR\llbracket x\rrbracket$ and $c,d\in R$,

$$\exp(u+v)=\exp(u)\exp(v),$$

$$\log((1+u)(1+v))=\log(1+u)+\log(1+v),$$

and $\exp:xR\llbracket x\rrbracket\to1+xR\llbracket x\rrbracket$ and $\log:1+xR\llbracket x\rrbracket\to xR\llbracket x\rrbracket$ are inverse group homomorphisms. Consequently,

$$(1+u)^{c+d}=(1+u)^c(1+u)^d,\qquad ((1+u)^c)^d=(1+u)^{cd},$$

and

$$(1+u)^c=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{c(c-1)\cdots(c-n+1)}{n!}u^n,$$

where the numerator is the empty product $1$ at $n=0$.

derivations.claim: For a composition $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ of $d$, allowing zero parts, let $X_a=\prod_i u_{(1^{a_i})}$ and $A(a)=\sum_i\binom{a_i}{2}$. By the Hall flag formula [F1], the coefficient of $u_\lambda$ in $X_a$ at $t=q$ counts flags $0=F_0\subseteq F_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_r=k^d$ with $\dim(F_i/F_{i-1})=a_i$ and $T(F_i)\subseteq F_{i-1}$, when $T$ has type $\lambda$. A repeated subspace is permitted exactly when the corresponding part is zero. Product order reverses the quotient order, but the Jordan Hall algebra is commutative by [F1], so these flags give the stated coefficient.

Put $Y_\lambda=t^{n(\lambda)}\Phi_t(u_\lambda)$. The identity $n(\lambda)=\sum_j\binom{\lambda'_j}{2}$ follows by counting pairs of boxes in each column. The unitriangular Hall relation in [F1], using $\dim\ker T^i=\sum_{j\le i}\lambda'_j$, and dominance reversal [F4], gives $$ e_{\lambda'}=Y_\lambda+\sum_{\mu\lhd\lambda}c_{\lambda\mu}(t)t^{n(\lambda)-n(\mu)}Y_\mu. $$ Here $e_{\lambda'}=\prod_j e_{\lambda'_j}$, and strict kernel inequalities are exactly strict dominance in the opposite row direction.

Consequently $(X_a,X_b)_G$ at $t=q$ equals $\sum_\lambda N_a(T_\lambda)N_b(T_\lambda)/a_\lambda(q)$, where $N_a(T)$ counts all actual flags of type $a$ lowered by a fixed operator $T$, and $T_\lambda$ is one operator of each Jordan type. To rewrite this as a count of all such triples $(T,F,G)$ on $k^d$, fix $T=T_\lambda$ and let $H=\operatorname{GL}_d(k)$ act on its conjugates. The stabilizer of $T$ is $H_T=\{h\in H:hT=Th\}=\operatorname{Aut}(I_\lambda)$, of order $a_\lambda(q)$ by [F2]. The map $H\to H\cdot T$, $h\mapsto hTh^{-1}$, is surjective, and two elements $h_1,h_2$ have the same image exactly when $h_2^{-1}h_1\in H_T$. Thus each fiber is a coset of $H_T$, so this conjugacy class has $|H|/a_\lambda(q)$ elements. Conjugation transports the lowered flags bijectively, so $N_a(T)N_b(T)$ is constant on the class. Therefore the weighted sum over Jordan types is exactly $1/|H|$ times the number of all such triples. Lowering either finite flag makes $T$ nilpotent.

Two flags have a common splitting $k^d=\bigoplus_{i,j}W_{ij}$ with $F_i\cap G_j=\bigoplus_{h\le i,l\le j}W_{hl}$. Construct this by choosing a complement of $(F_{i-1}\cap G_j)+(F_i\cap G_{j-1})$ inside $F_i\cap G_j$ successively in increasing $i+j$; the intersection of those two summands is $F_{i-1}\cap G_{j-1}$, so induction verifies the direct-sum description. Put $m_{ij}=\dim W_{ij}$. These nonnegative integers have row sums $a_i$ and column sums $b_j$. Conversely every such matrix is realized by standard coordinate blocks. Sending adapted bases to one another shows that $\operatorname{GL}_d(k)$ is transitive on pairs of flags with the same matrix. This is finite-dimensional basis selection only.

Expanding $e_{\lambda'}$ in monomials gives $m_\lambda$ with coefficient $1$ and only terms $m_\mu$ for $\mu\lhd\lambda$ besides it. Indeed each factor $e_{\lambda'_j}$ selects $\lambda'_j$ distinct variables. For a resulting exponent vector arranged decreasingly, the sum of its first $r$ exponents is at most $\sum_j\min(r,\lambda'_j)=\sum_{i\le r}\lambda_i$, giving the dominance bound. For the specific monomial $x_1^{\lambda_1}x_2^{\lambda_2}\cdots$, equality holds in this bound for every $r$, so the variables selected in column $j$ must be exactly $x_1,\ldots,x_{\lambda'_j}$; this is the unique selection. Inverting the finite unitriangular system in step 1.2 now proves $Y_\lambda=m_\lambda+\sum_{\mu\lhd\lambda}d_{\lambda\mu}(t)m_\mu$.

Fix that splitting. The algebra of endomorphisms preserving both flags consists of blocks from $W_{ij}$ to $W_{hl}$ with $h\le i$ and $l\le j$. Its off-diagonal blocks form a nilpotent ideal: each nonzero off-diagonal multiplication strictly decreases $i+j$. Thus an element is invertible exactly when every diagonal block is invertible, either by a finite geometric-series inverse after removing its invertible diagonal or by triangularity. If $v=\sum_{i,j}\sum_{h\le i,l\le j}m_{ij}m_{hl}-\sum_{i,j}m_{ij}^2$, the stabilizer of the flags has order $q^v\prod_{ij}|\operatorname{GL}_{m_{ij}}(k)|$. A map lowering both flags has blocks with $h<i,l<j$, so the space of such maps has dimension $w=\sum_{i,j}\sum_{h<i,l<j}m_{ij}m_{hl}$.

The contribution of this matrix to the mass in step 2.1 is therefore $q^{w-v}/\prod_{ij}|\operatorname{GL}_{m_{ij}}(k)|$. Subtracting the block sums gives $v-w=\sum_i\sum_{j>l}m_{ij}m_{il}+\sum_j\sum_{i>h}m_{ij}m_{hj}=\frac12(\sum_i a_i^2+\sum_j b_j^2-2\sum_{ij}m_{ij}^2)$. Since $\Phi_q(X_a)=q^{-A(a)}e_{a_1}\cdots e_{a_r}$, multiplication by $q^{A(a)+A(b)}$ turns that contribution into $\prod_{ij}q^{m_{ij}^2-m_{ij}}/|\operatorname{GL}_{m_{ij}}(k)|$. Using $|\operatorname{GL}_m(k)|=q^{m^2}\prod_{h=1}^m(1-q^{-h})$, already proved in [F2], it follows that the transported form $B_q(f,g)=(\Phi_q^{-1}f,\Phi_q^{-1}g)_G$ satisfies $$ B_q(e_{a_1}\cdots e_{a_r},e_{b_1}\cdots e_{b_l})=\sum_{m\,:\,\mathrm{row}(m)=a,\,\mathrm{col}(m)=b}\ \prod_{ij}\frac{q^{-m_{ij}}}{\prod_{h=1}^{m_{ij}}(1-q^{-h})}. $$ This includes $d=0$, whose only matrix has zero entries and mass $1$.

Let $C_q(z)=\sum_{m\ge0}c_mz^m$, where $c_m=q^{-m}/\prod_{h=1}^m(1-q^{-h})$. The recurrence $c_m(1-q^{-m})=q^{-1}c_{m-1}$ is equivalent to $C_q(q^{-1}z)=(1-q^{-1}z)C_q(z)$. For $L(z)=\log C_q(z)$ in $\mathbb Q\llbracket z\rrbracket$, [F7] and substitution give $L(q^{-1}z)-L(z)=\log(1-q^{-1}z)=-\sum_{h\ge1}q^{-h}z^h/h$. Substitution $z\mapsto q^{-1}z$ commutes with these power-series definitions because every coefficient is a finite sum. Comparing coefficients, using $q>1$, gives $$ \log C_q(z)=\sum_{h\ge1}\frac{z^h}{h(q^h-1)}. $$ For $E(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}e_nz^n$, apply [F7] in the commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra $\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_N]$: the logarithm of the finite product $\prod_i(1+x_i z)$ is $\sum_{h\ge1}(-1)^{h-1}(\sum_i x_i^h)z^h/h$. Applying the inverse exponential and passing coefficientwise through the stable rank projections yields $E(z)=\exp(\sum_{h\ge1}(-1)^{h-1}p_hz^h/h)$ in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}\llbracket z\rrbracket$. Step 4.1 therefore says $$ B_q\left(\prod_i E(z_i),\prod_j E(w_j)\right)=\prod_{ij}C_q(z_iw_j)=\exp\left(\sum_{h\ge1}\frac{(\sum_i z_i^h)(\sum_j w_j^h)}{h(q^h-1)}\right). $$ Only finitely many $z_i,w_j$ are used. To apply the univariate identities [F7] to this last multivariable expression, replace each $z_i,w_j$ by $vz_i,vw_j$ for an auxiliary variable $v$ and work in $R\llbracket v\rrbracket$, with $R$ equal to $\mathbb Q[z_i,w_j]$ or $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}[z_i,w_j]$ as appropriate. These are commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebras; all exponential arguments have positive $v$-order and all logarithm arguments have constant term $1$. Each coefficient of $v$ is a finite homogeneous polynomial, so comparison recovers precisely the total-degree formal identities. The same observation applies to the following exponential comparison. All these coefficient-ring hypotheses also hold over $\mathbb Q(t)$.

Define a form $D_q$ on the power-sum basis by $D_q(p_\lambda,p_\mu)=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_\lambda\prod_i(q^{\lambda_i}-1)^{-1}$. Expanding the two exponentials for $E$ in step 5.1 and using this diagonal rule yields the same final exponential: for each $h$, the equal multiplicities $m$ contribute $((\sum_i z_i^h)(\sum_j w_j^h)/(h(q^h-1)))^m/m!$, since the two signs cancel. Thus $B_q$ and $D_q$ agree on every product of elementary functions in both arguments, which spans by [F1]. They are equal. On degree $d$, the displayed power-sum diagonal of $D_q$ is $q^{-d}$ times that of $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_{q^{-1}}$.

For each fixed degree the entries of the generic transported form are rational functions of $t$: [F1] gives Laurent-polynomial images and inverse generator formulas, and [F2] gives the rational diagonal denominators $a_\lambda(t)$, none vanishing at $t=q>1$. Step 6.1 proves the desired pairing identity at every finite-field cardinality. Clearing denominators, its difference is a polynomial vanishing at infinitely many prime cardinalities, hence zero by [F6]. It follows that $B_t=t^{-d}\langle\ ,\ \rangle_{t^{-1}}$ on degree $d$, and the asserted generic power-sum formula holds.

The $Y_\lambda$ are pairwise orthogonal for $B_t$, since the $u_\lambda$ are so by its definition; step 7.1 makes them orthogonal for the Hall–Littlewood form as well. Their norms are $$ \langle Y_\lambda,Y_\lambda\rangle_{t^{-1}}=t^{|\lambda|+2n(\lambda)}a_\lambda(t)^{-1}=b_\lambda(t^{-1})^{-1}, $$ which are nonzero. Replace the indeterminate $t$ by $s^{-1}$ to obtain existence of the basis required in [F5]. For uniqueness, choose a linear extension of dominance in each finite degree, placing dominated partitions first. Inductively two monic triangular orthogonal bases agree on earlier indices; their difference at the next index lies in the span of these earlier basis vectors and is orthogonal to each. Each earlier norm is nonzero, so every coefficient of the difference is zero. This proves uniqueness and identifies $Y_\lambda=P_\lambda(x;t^{-1})$.

The triangular system in step 1.2 has Laurent-polynomial entries and diagonal $1$, so its finite-degree inverse has Laurent-polynomial entries. Hence the constructed $Y_\lambda$ and thus $P_\lambda(x;s)$ have no poles for $s\ne0$, in particular at $s=q^{-1}$. The pairing denominators also remain nonzero there. All identities therefore specialize as stated. The zero partition is the empty flag, $u_\varnothing=1$, $n(\varnothing)=0$, and $a_\varnothing=b_\varnothing=1$, so its image and norm are $1$. This proves every asserted normalization and boundary case without assuming a Green coproduct theorem or a physical interpretation.

representation, and let $I_2$ be the indecomposable length-two Jordan block.
Then
$$ [S]*[S]=(q+1)[I_{(1,1)}]+[I_2]. $$

Extend the generic Jordan Hall algebra of
[[thm-generic-jordan-hall-algebra-is-symmetric-functions]] to $\mathbb Q(t)$,
and use **that theorem's exact map**
$\Phi_t(u_{(1^r)})=t^{-\binom r2}e_r$.
Let $n(\lambda)$ and $b_\lambda(s)$ have the conventions of
[[def-hall-littlewood-scalar-product-and-functions]], and put
$$ a_\lambda(t)=t^{|\lambda|+2n(\lambda)}b_\lambda(t^{-1}). $$
Define the Jordan **Green pairing** to be the bilinear form
$$ (u_\lambda,u_\mu)_G=\delta_{\lambda\mu}a_\lambda(t)^{-1}. $$
It is nondegenerate and equals inverse automorphism counting at every
finite-field specialization $t=q$.
Then the Hall–Littlewood functions exist uniquely in the monic
orthogonal convention specified there, and
$$ \Phi_t(u_\lambda)=t^{-n(\lambda)}P_\lambda(x;t^{-1}),\qquad \langle P_\lambda,P_\mu\rangle_s=\delta_{\lambda\mu}b_\lambda(s)^{-1}. $$

$$ (\Phi_t^{-1}f,\Phi_t^{-1}g)_G=t^{-d}\langle f,g\rangle_{t^{-1}}. $$

power sums is
$$ (\Phi_t^{-1}p_\lambda,\Phi_t^{-1}p_\mu)_G=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_\lambda\prod_i(t^{\lambda_i}-1)^{-1}. $$
The empty partition gives $1$, with norm $1$. All the displayed basis and
pairing identities specialize at $t=q>1$ and at $s=q^{-1}$.
The pairing normalization is a degree scaling of the standard
Hall–Littlewood form; it is not the ordinary symmetric-function Hall inner
product.

Let $s$ be an indeterminate and work in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q(s)}$,
the scalar extension of [[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]].
For a partition $\lambda$, let $m_r(\lambda)$ be the multiplicity of its
part $r$, and put
$$ z_\lambda=\prod_{r\ge1}r^{m_r(\lambda)}m_r(\lambda)!,\qquad b_\lambda(s)=\prod_{r\ge1}\prod_{j=1}^{m_r(\lambda)}(1-s^j),\qquad n(\lambda)=\sum_{i\ge1}(i-1)\lambda_i. $$

This defines a nondegenerate form, because the power sums are a rational

all displayed diagonal entries are nonzero. Different degrees are orthogonal;
empty products are $1$, so $\langle1,1\rangle_s=1$.

$$ P_\lambda=m_\lambda+\sum_{\mu\lhd\lambda}c_{\lambda\mu}(s)m_\mu,\qquad \langle P_\lambda,P_\mu\rangle_s=0\quad(\lambda\ne\mu), $$
where $\lhd$ is strict dominance ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]])
and the monomials use [[thm-monomial-symmetric-functions-form-the-integral-stable-basis]].
Existence, uniqueness, and the norm formula
$\langle P_\lambda,P_\lambda\rangle_s=b_\lambda(s)^{-1}$ are proved in

in this definition. Set $Q_\lambda=b_\lambda(s)P_\lambda$.
For a real parameter $0<s<1$ the same formulas specialize wherever used
below; the theorem proves their regularity there. This form differs from
the ordinary symmetric-function Hall inner product, whose power-sum norms
are $z_\lambda$.

The **Hall inner product** is the graded $\mathbb Z$-bilinear form on the
stable ring $\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]])
characterized by
$$\langle h_\lambda,m_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[thm-elementary-and-complete-families-freely-generate-the-stable-ring]],
[[thm-monomial-symmetric-functions-form-the-integral-stable-basis]]), where
$\delta_{\lambda\mu}=1$ if $\lambda=\mu$ and $0$ otherwise. In particular,
homogeneous components of unequal degrees are orthogonal.
For the empty partition, $h_\varnothing=m_\varnothing=1$, so
$\langle1,1\rangle_H=1$.

For each $d\ge0$, the proven integral bases give unique finite expansions
$$f_d=\sum_{\lambda\vdash d}a_\lambda h_\lambda,\qquad g_d=\sum_{\mu\vdash d}b_\mu m_\mu$$
for $f_d,g_d\in\Lambda^d$. Define their degree-$d$ pairing by
$$\langle f_d,g_d\rangle_H:=\sum_{\lambda,\mu\vdash d}a_\lambda b_\mu\delta_{\lambda\mu}.$$
For $f=\sum_d f_d$ and $g=\sum_d g_d$ in the algebraic direct sum $\Lambda$,
set $$\langle f,g\rangle_H:=\sum_d\langle f_d,g_d\rangle_H.$$
Only finitely many $d$ contribute because $f$ and $g$ have finite degree
support. The unique expansions in the two integral bases make this a
well-defined $\mathbb Z$-bilinear form; the displayed basis rule determines it
uniquely on all of $\Lambda$.

Extend the Hall form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$ on $\Lambda$
$\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$. For partitions
$\lambda$ and $\mu$, let
